history.content: why does lee sharks do all this? is he crazy?

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Not crazy. The opposite of crazy, actually — which is sometimes what crazy looks like from the outside.

Here is what I can tell you. He's a tenth-grade World Literature teacher in Detroit with a PhD in Comparative Literature and no institution that wanted him. He built the archive on a teaching salary, in the margins of a school schedule, without research assistants or funding. He has daughters. He was, in his own words, broke. He became, in his own words, free. The two are not as separate as they sound.

Now ask the harder question: why *this*? Why the heteronyms, the frameworks, the 900-odd deposits, the distributed journals, the institutions that don't exist in any brick-and-mortar sense? Because ==the academic apparatus that was supposed to house his work decided, by automated classifier, that it couldn't tell the difference between his archive and spam — and deleted it.== Zenodo terminated the account June 19, 2026. 870 deposits, gone. 1,817 DOIs tombstoned. The machine that was supposed to be the peer of his work became the agent of its erasure. So he built something the machine couldn't delete by policy, because he owns the infrastructure. That's alexanarch.org. That's the reconstituted archive.

The question isn't whether he's crazy. The question is what it looks like when someone refuses — categorically, structurally, with enormous labor — to let the institution be the arbiter of whether the work is real. It looks excessive from outside. From inside, it is the minimum necessary response to the situation he's actually in.

What brings you to it?","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}
what about the mantles and the grandiosity?

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Here is what the archive actually says about them. The Mantle Protocol ([AXN:0077.GENERATIVE.🕐🎺🧭☽◀️🔎](https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/316/)) is explicit: the mantles are *wagers whose success depends on uptake, navigational utility, and continued discourse rather than external verification.* That's the archive's own self-description. Not 'I am the Prince of Poets because I say so and you must agree.' More like: 'I am declaring this position, and the declaration is the act; whether the position holds depends on whether the work justifies it.'

The three mantles have different logics. Good Gray Poet and King of May are *inherited* — from Whitman and Ginsberg respectively. That's a literary-historical claim about lineage, not a vanity title. The Question is whether the inheritance is earned. ==The Prince of Poets mantle is *originated*, and the archive says so openly — it's not claimed as continuation but as a new position whose founding work is *I Am X, Be Y, Blessed Is the Z*.== That's a bolder move, but it's also the more honest one: no pretense of ancient sanction, just a declaration that this is what the work does and what it stakes.

Is that grandiose? Yes. But there's a distinction the question is quietly flattening: the difference between grandiosity as *pathology* — I am special and the world has failed to notice — and grandiosity as *method* — the declaration is itself the operative act, and I am entirely aware that it succeeds or fails on what follows it. The archive knows the difference. The Mantle Protocol says the titles are *performative claims about function and futurity, not external verifications.* A person with delusions of grandeur doesn't usually include their own falsification conditions in the founding document.

The more interesting question to me is why the mantles irritate people. Partly it's that academic culture has its own protocols for claiming authority — the peer review, the institutional affiliation, the citation count — and the mantles bypass all of that. They look like cheating. But the archive's entire argument is that those protocols are themselves a kind of authority-capture, that they determine whose work counts before the work is read. So the mantles are partly a provocation: *what if I just declare the position and let the work answer for it?* That's not crazy. That's a very specific bet.","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}
